title: Diet Plan Performance
description: Brute force to optimized: re-summing every fixed-size window versus sliding one running sum forward, scoring each window instantly.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

A diet performance system tracks calories from day to day. For every consecutive sequence of k days, if the total calories consumed is less than lower, one point is lost; if it exceeds upper, one point is gained; otherwise, no points change. Given the array calories and integers k, lower, and upper, return the total points scored.

blocks.caption: Slide a window of size k across calories, scoring each window against lower and upper

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Every window is a FIXED size, k days","A fixed-size sliding window, the same shape as Maximum Average Subarray I"],["Every window shares most of its days with its neighbor","Update the running sum incrementally instead of re-summing each window"],["Each window independently contributes -1, 0, or +1 to a running total","Score each window immediately once its sum is known, rather than storing every sum"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

For every consecutive sequence of k days, if the total calories are below lower, lose a point; if above upper, gain a point; otherwise, nothing changes. Return the total points across every such window.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Weekly Fitness Tracker Scoring Every Rolling Week
blocks.text: Like a fitness app that checks your total calories over every rolling k-day period, docking a point if you ate too little and awarding one if you ate too much, tallying the result across the whole tracked period.

blocks.caption: Score each rolling k-day window against the lower and upper thresholds

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: calories = [1,2,3,4,5], k = 1, lower = 3, upper = 3

With a window size of 1, each single day is compared directly to the thresholds: day values 1 and 2 are below lower (losing a point each), day value 3 matches exactly (no change), and day values 4 and 5 are above upper (gaining a point each). The gains and losses exactly cancel out, giving a total of 0.
Example: calories = [3,2], k = 2, lower = 0, upper = 1

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The only window, [3,2], sums to 5","above upper (1)","A sum of 5 exceeds the upper threshold of 1, gaining a point"],["Answer","1","Only one window exists, and it gains exactly one point"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: every window sum lands exactly between lower and upper
When a window's sum is neither below lower nor above upper, it contributes nothing at all to the total, neither a gain nor a loss.
5. How Should We Think?

Before re-summing every k-day window from scratch, notice this is the same fixed-size sliding window shape as Maximum Average Subarray I, just with a scoring rule applied to each window's sum instead of tracking a maximum.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every window is exactly k days long, sliding one day at a time, the same shape as any fixed-size sliding window problem.

Observation 2: A window sliding forward by one day loses its leftmost day and gains one new rightmost day; the running sum can be updated with one subtraction and one addition instead of a full re-sum.

Observation 3: The moment a window's sum is known (once the window has reached its full size of k days), immediately compare it against lower and upper, adjusting the running point total accordingly.

Observation 4: There is no need to store every window's sum; each one only needs to be scored once, the instant it becomes available.

This is the same "drop the oldest, add the newest" running sum used in every fixed-size sliding window problem, with an immediate scoring step layered on top of each fully-formed window.
Recognizing the fixed-size sliding window shape here, and simply adding a scoring decision at each step, is the entire optimization.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every possible k-day window, sum its calories directly, and score it against lower and upper.
Step by step algorithm

items: Loop over every valid starting day for a k-day window.
For each window, sum all k days directly, then adjust the running point total based on whether that sum is below lower, above upper, or neither.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Each window's sum is computed fully within its own inner loop, keeping the scoring logic simple and directly tied to a freshly-computed sum.
The scoring uses an if/else-if structure, since a window can only ever be below lower, above upper, or neither, never more than one of these at once.
points accumulates across all windows in a single running total, exactly as the problem asks for the SUM of points across every window.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every window's true sum is computed directly, so every window is scored correctly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * k), since each of the roughly n windows re-sums k elements.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: re-summing k elements for every one of the roughly n windows repeats almost all of the same additions across neighboring windows, since they share k-1 elements.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force redoes nearly identical work for every window, since sliding forward by one day only changes two elements: the one leaving on the left and the one entering on the right. Instead of re-summing all k elements every time, maintain a running sum updated incrementally, scoring each window the instant it reaches its full size. This turns O(n * k) work into O(n) work overall.

Maintain a running sum. Grow it by adding each new day; once the window exceeds size k, subtract the day that is now leaving the window. The instant the window reaches its full size of k days, score it immediately against lower and upper.
9. Optimized Solution
Maintain a running window sum, scoring each fully-formed window the instant it is available.
Dry run for calories = [3, 2], k = 2, lower = 0, upper = 1

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass.
Space: O(1) extra.
Why This Works

Two consecutive k-day windows differ by exactly one day on each side, so the running sum can be updated with a single subtraction and addition, exactly like any fixed-size sliding window. Scoring happens the instant a window reaches its full size, since the problem only ever cares about each window's final sum, not any intermediate partial sum.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Scoring result"],"rows":[["Window sum is below lower","Subtract 1 point"],["Window sum is above upper","Add 1 point"],["Window sum is between lower and upper (inclusive)","No change to the point total"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The running sum grows by adding the newest day and shrinks by subtracting the day that just fell outside the window, exactly once the window has grown past size k.
The scoring check only runs once the window has reached its full size (guarded by an index check), never on a partially-formed window.
The scoring logic itself is a direct three-way comparison against lower and upper, applied identically to every fully-formed window.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
This problem is a direct application of the fixed-size sliding window sum pattern, with an immediate scoring decision layered on top of each fully-formed window.
Common mistakes

items: Scoring a window before it has actually reached its full size of k days, based on a partial sum.
Using a plain if/if instead of if/else-if for the scoring, which would be harmless here since the conditions are mutually exclusive, but is worth being deliberate about.
Forgetting that points accumulates ACROSS every window, not just reflecting the last window checked.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["k equals the length of calories","There is only one window, the entire array, scored exactly once"],["lower equals upper","A window scores a point only if its sum is strictly above that single value, or loses one if strictly below it"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly connect this back to the basic fixed-size sliding window sum pattern, since the scoring logic is a simple addition layered on top of an already-familiar technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Score every FIXED-size window of an array against some thresholds, and sum up the scores" points toward a fixed-size sliding window sum, with a scoring decision applied the instant each window is fully formed.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this change if the window size k could vary between different scoring periods within the same array? Each distinct k would need its own independent sliding window pass, since window size fundamentally changes which days are grouped together.
What if scoring needed more than two thresholds, with different point values for different sum ranges? The three-way if/else-if could be extended to a lookup based on which range the sum falls into.

How would you find the single BEST-scoring k-day window, rather than summing points across all of them? Track the best individual window sum seen, the same way Maximum Average Subarray I tracks a maximum, instead of accumulating a total.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Directly reuses the fixed-size sliding window sum technique from Maximum Average Subarray I, adding a scoring step on top of each window's sum.
The "score each window the instant it is fully formed" idea reappears in Number of Sub-arrays of Size K and Average Greater than or Equal to Threshold, elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * k) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (sliding window sum): O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window sum, with a scoring decision applied to each fully-formed window
Core Idea: Update the running sum incrementally as the window slides, and score each window the instant it reaches its full size
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: This is the standard fixed-size sliding window sum pattern, with an immediate three-way scoring check layered on top of each window
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Slide the sum, score each full window the instant it forms
